one-quantitative-displays-s1.title: Books read over the summer

plot.label: Dotplot of the number of books each of 25 students read over the summer, from 0 to 12 books

one-quantitative-displays-s1.text: A teacher asked 25 students how many books they read over the summer. Each dot is one student (invented data).

one-quantitative-displays-s2.title: Scores on a chemistry test
one-quantitative-displays-s2.text: A stemplot of the scores of 20 students on a chemistry test (invented data). Key: 7 | 4 stands for 74 points.

one-quantitative-displays-s3.title: Commute times of 200 workers
one-quantitative-displays-s3.text: A cumulative relative frequency graph of the one-way commute times of 200 workers at a company. Each point gives the proportion of workers whose commute is that many minutes or less (invented data).

items.q: How many of the students read more than 6 books?

why.correct: Count the dots to the right of 6: one each at 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12, so 5 students.
options: More than 6 leaves out the two dots at 6.
Right: one dot each at 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12.
6 is a number of books on the axis; count the dots to the right of it.
12 is the largest value, not a count of students.

items.q: What proportion of the 25 students read 0, 1, 2 or 3 books?

why.correct: Dots at 0, 1, 2 and 3: $1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12$, so the proportion is $\frac{12}{25} = 0.48$.

mistakes.why: That counts just the five students who read 3 books. Add the dots at 0, 1, 2 and 3: 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12.
That also counts the four students at 4 (16 of 25). Stop at 3 books: 12 of 25.

items.q: The teacher makes a histogram with bins 0 to 2, 2 to 4, 4 to 6 and so on, where each bin holds its left end and not its right end. How many students fall in the 2 to 4 bin?

why.correct: The 2 to 4 bin holds the values 2 and 3: $4 + 5 = 9$ students.
options: A value of 4 is the right end of the 2 to 4 bin, so it belongs in the 4 to 6 bin.
The bin starts at 2, so it also holds the four students who read 2 books.
The width of a bin is 2 books; the height is the number of students in it.
Right: the bin holds the 4 students at 2 and the 5 at 3, and the students at 4 go in the next bin.

items.q: Why is a dotplot a good choice for these data?

why.correct: For a small quantitative data set, a dotplot shows every value on a number line.
options: Right: with 25 values a dotplot shows each value and how often it occurs.
A dotplot needs a number line, so it is for quantitative data.
A dotplot shows every value, including the largest ones.
With hundreds of values the dots pile up; a histogram is then easier to read.
There are few values, so every student can be seen
Dotplots work for categorical data such as favorite authors
A dotplot gets rid of the students who read the most books
A dotplot works for any data set, whatever the number of values

why.correct: Each score is a stem (tens) joined to a leaf (ones): the first row, 5 | 8, is 58.
options: 5 is a stem, the tens digit. Join it to its leaf: 58.
8 is a leaf, the ones digit. With stem 5 it is 58.
Right: the stem 5 with leaf 8 is 58.
The row for stem 5 has one score, 58, which is lower than 62.

items.q: How many students scored in the 80s?

why.correct: Count the leaves on the 8 stem: 0, 1, 3, 4, 4, 6, 8, so 7 students.
options: Two students scored 84, so the leaf 4 appears twice and both count.
8 is the stem for the eighties; count the leaves on that row.
Right: the stem 8 has seven leaves: 0, 1, 3, 4, 4, 6, 8.
The nineties are the next row, stem 9.

items.q: What proportion of the 20 students scored 90 or above?

mistakes.why: That is the count. Divide by the 20 students: 3/20.
That counts the 80s and 90s together. Scores of 90 or above are the stem 9 row: 3 of 20.

items.q: What does this stemplot show that a histogram with bins of 10 points would not?

why.correct: A stemplot keeps every data value; a histogram groups values into bins and shows only how many fall in each.
options: Right: the leaves keep every value, while a histogram shows only counts in each bin.
A histogram with bins of 10 shows those counts too.
Both displays let you count the 20 students.
A histogram shows this as its tallest bar.
The exact score of each student
How many students scored in each group of ten points
The number of students who took the chemistry test
Which range of ten points holds the largest number of scores

items.q: What proportion of the workers commute 20 minutes or less?

why.correct: A cumulative relative frequency graph gives, at each value, the proportion of the data at or below it: 0.45 at 20 minutes.
options: That is the proportion between 10 and 20 minutes. "Or less" is the height at 20 itself.
That is 1 − 0.45, the workers who commute longer than 20 minutes.
20 minutes is the value on the horizontal axis; read the height above it.
Right: at 20 minutes the graph reads 0.45.

items.q: What proportion of the workers commute more than 30 minutes?

why.correct: More than 30 is what is left after the 0.70 at or below 30: $1 - 0.70 = 0.30$.
options: 0.70 is the proportion at or below 30 minutes. The question asks about the rest.
Right: 0.70 commute 30 minutes or less, so $1 - 0.70 = 0.30$ commute more.
That is just the workers from 30 to 40 minutes; more than 30 includes everyone above 30.
0.85 is the proportion at or below 40 minutes.

items.q: What proportion of the workers commute more than 20 minutes and up to 40 minutes?

why.correct: The proportion between two values is the difference of the graph’s heights: $0.85 - 0.45 = 0.40$.
options: Right: subtract the heights, $0.85 - 0.45 = 0.40$.
Heights are subtracted, not added: the proportion up to 40 minus the proportion up to 20.
That includes the workers at 20 minutes or less too.
20 is the number of minutes between 20 and 40; the proportion comes from the heights.

items.q: Half of the workers commute this many minutes or less. Between which two times on the graph is it?

why.correct: Find where the graph crosses 0.50. It is at 0.45 at 20 minutes and 0.70 at 30, so between 20 and 30.
options: At 20 minutes only 0.45 of workers have been counted, so the halfway point comes after 20.
The middle of the axis is not the middle of the data; the graph reaches 0.50 before 30.
Right: the graph passes 0.50 between its heights of 0.45 at 20 and 0.70 at 30.
By 40 minutes the graph is already at 0.85, well past half.
Between 10 and 20 minutes, near 15
Exactly 30 minutes, the middle of the axis
Between 20 and 30 minutes
Between 40 and 50 minutes, where the line flattens

items.q: A histogram of 500 race finishing times uses bins 10 minutes wide. What happens if the bins are made 2 minutes wide?

why.correct: A histogram’s look depends on its bin width: narrow bins show detail and noise, wide bins smooth it away.
options: Narrower bins hold fewer values each, so the bars get shorter, not taller.
Right: narrow bins split the data more finely, so small ups and downs appear.
Every runner is still in exactly one bin; only the grouping changes.
That is what wider bins do.
The same bars as before, each bar 5 times as tall
More, shorter bars that show finer detail and more bumps
The number of runners changes, since bins change
Fewer, wider bars that give a smoother picture of the data

items.q: Which display is most practical for the heights of 2,000 adults?

why.correct: For large quantitative data sets, a histogram summarizes by bins; dotplots and stemplots suit small data sets.
options: Two thousand dots would pile into tall, unreadable stacks.
A stemplot with 2,000 leaves would be far too long.
A pie chart is for categories; heights are quantitative.
Right: it groups the 2,000 values into bins, so the display stays readable.
A dotplot with one dot for each adult
A stemplot with one leaf for each adult
A pie chart with one slice for each height
A histogram

items.q: Why do the bars of a histogram touch, unlike the bars of a bar chart?

why.correct: A histogram’s bins are consecutive intervals of a number line, so the bars touch; a bar chart’s categories are separate.
options: The order the data were collected is not shown in a histogram.
Right: the bins cover a number line with no breaks, so the bars meet.
A histogram shows a quantitative variable.
Touching bars come from the number line, not from the drawing style.
To show that the values were collected one after another in time
Its horizontal axis is a number line split into bins
Because a histogram shows a categorical variable
To make the histogram easier to color and to label

items.q: A histogram shows the counts of 40 commute times in bins 5 minutes wide. Which of these can be read from the histogram? Select all that apply.

why.correct: A histogram keeps counts per bin, and so the total, but not individual values.
options: Right: that is the height of each bar.
The histogram shows only which bin the longest commute is in.
Right: the bar heights add to 40.
A histogram does not keep individual values or their order.
How many commutes are in each 5-minute bin
The exact length of the longest commute
The total number of commutes, by adding the bars
The commute time of each worker in the order asked
